Part 2 (modB) · Linear Algebra and Geometry · Channels A, B and C · Lesson L02

Complex numbers I

The equation x2=−1x^2 = -1x2=−1 has no real solutions. By adding a single new symbol, the imaginary unit iii with i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1, you get the field C\CC of complex numbers. Here you learn to compute with the numbers a+bia + bia+bi (sums, products, conjugate, modulus, inverse, divisions) and to see them as points of the plane. In every exam session from 2024 to 2026 there is at least one quiz question that starts from these computations.

lesson 2 · pp. 6–9

The lesson in 8 points

  • No real number solves x2=−1x^2 = -1x2=−1. The complex numbers add to the reals a new symbol, the imaginary unit iii, with a single new rule: i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1.
  • A complex number is written z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi with a,b∈Ra, b \in \Ra,b∈R. The real number aaa is the real part Re⁡(z)\operatorname{Re}(z)Re(z), the real number bbb (without the iii) is the imaginary part Im⁡(z)\operatorname{Im}(z)Im(z).
  • You add real part to real part and imaginary part to imaginary part. You multiply as with letters, then replace i2i^2i2 with −1-1−1: (7+i)(4−i)=29−3i(7 + i)(4 - i) = 29 - 3i(7+i)(4−i)=29−3i.
  • C\CC is a field, with the same nine properties as R\RR, but it is not ordered: between two complex numbers it makes no sense to say which one is bigger.
  • The conjugate of z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi is zˉ=a−bi\bar z = a - bizˉ=a−bi. The modulus is the real number ∣z∣=a2+b2|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}∣z∣=a2+b2​, and zzˉ=∣z∣2z\bar z = |z|^2zzˉ=∣z∣2 holds.
  • Every z≠0z \neq 0z=0 has an inverse z−1=zˉ∣z∣2z^{-1} = \frac{\bar z}{|z|^2}z−1=∣z∣2zˉ​. To divide, you multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
  • Complex numbers are the points of the complex plane: a+bia + bia+bi is the point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b), the sum follows the parallelogram rule, the modulus is the distance from the origin.
  • At the exam: in three exam sessions question 1 of the quiz was an equation like (1+i)z=3+2i(1 + i)z = 3 + 2i(1+i)z=3+2i, to be solved precisely with the conjugate.

Channels A, B and C

The Linear Algebra and Geometry handouts are the same for channels A, B and C (Buzano teaches in channels A and B, Radeschi in channels B and C), so these notes hold for all three. Only the days of the lessons change: the announcements are on the course's Moodle page (MDAG2, id 3831). Exam and quiz are the same for everyone.

§1

Why we need complex numbers

p. 6

In lesson L01 you saw that every new number set arises from an equation that has no solution in the old set. The last row of that table was

x2=−1.x^2 = -1.x2=−1.

No real number solves it, because the square of a real number is never negative:

  • if x≥0x \ge 0x≥0, then x2=x⋅x≥0x^2 = x \cdot x \ge 0x2=x⋅x≥0;
  • if x<0x < 0x<0, then −x-x−x is positive and x2=(−x)⋅(−x)>0x^2 = (-x) \cdot (-x) > 0x2=(−x)⋅(−x)>0.

So x2+1≥1x^2 + 1 \ge 1x2+1≥1 for every x∈Rx \in \Rx∈R: it is never 000.

The handouts present the complex numbers as an extension of R\RR, "built with the aim of obtaining better algebraic properties". In practice you add to the reals a single new object, iii, whose square is −1-1−1, and you keep computing with the usual rules. The gain is large: in the complex numbers every polynomial equation of degree at least 1 has a solution. It is the fundamental theorem of algebra (lesson L04), and it is the reason why the course uses C\CC, for example when it looks for the eigenvalues of a matrix (lessons L17 and L18).

Beyond the handouts · where they really come from

Historically the complex numbers were born from equations of the third degree. In the sixteenth century Gerolamo Cardano published a formula to solve equations like x3=15x+4x^3 = 15x + 4x3=15x+4. Applied to this equation, the formula asks you to compute −121\sqrt{-121}−121​, which does not exist among the reals. Yet the equation has a very simple real solution, x=4x = 4x=4: indeed 43=644^3 = 6443=64 and 15⋅4+4=6415 \cdot 4 + 4 = 6415⋅4+4=64. Rafael Bombelli had the idea of computing with −121=11i\sqrt{-121} = 11i−121​=11i as if it were any other number: the formula becomes

x=2+11i3+2−11i3,x = \sqrt[3]{2 + 11i} + \sqrt[3]{2 - 11i},x=32+11i​+32−11i​,

and since (2+i)3=2+11i(2 + i)^3 = 2 + 11i(2+i)3=2+11i and (2−i)3=2−11i(2 - i)^3 = 2 - 11i(2−i)3=2−11i (you check it in exercise 1), you find x=(2+i)+(2−i)=4x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4x=(2+i)+(2−i)=4. The "imaginary" numbers served to find real numbers.

§2

What a complex number is

p. 6

Definition 2.1 · Complex numbers

A complex number is an algebraic object written in the following way:

a+bia + bia+bi

where aaa and bbb are arbitrary real numbers and iii is a new symbol called the imaginary unit.

Piece by piece:

  • a+bia + bia+bi is read "aaa plus bbb iii". It is a single number, built with two real numbers: the first, aaa, stands alone; the second, bbb, is multiplied by iii.
  • aaa and bbb are any reals: positive, negative, zero, fractions, roots. Writing bibibi means b⋅ib \cdot ib⋅i. One also writes ibibib, especially with roots: i3i\sqrt 3i3​ is clearer than 3i\sqrt 3 i3​i, where the iii might seem to be under the root.
  • iii is not a real number: it is a new symbol. The name "imaginary" is only historical. For us iii is an object you compute with following just one extra rule, which you will see shortly: i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1.
  • The +++ in a+bia + bia+bi cannot be "carried out": aaa and bibibi stay separate, as in 3+223 + 2\sqrt 23+22​ in lesson L01, which does not reduce to a single simpler number.

Here are the handouts' examples, with the two components highlighted:

Complex numberaaabbbRemark
7\sqrt 77​7\sqrt 77​000a real number is complex: 7=7+0i\sqrt 7 = \sqrt 7 + 0i7​=7​+0i
2+i2 + i2+i222111iii alone means 1⋅i1 \cdot i1⋅i
23i23i23i000232323the part without iii is missing: 23i=0+23i23i = 0 + 23i23i=0+23i
4−i4 - i4−i444−1-1−1−i-i−i means (−1)⋅i(-1) \cdot i(−1)⋅i
−1+πi-1 + \pi i−1+πi−1-1−1π\piπbbb too can be irrational

Two special cases come up often:

  • if b=0b = 0b=0, the number a+0i=aa + 0i = aa+0i=a is a real number: the reals are contained in the complex numbers;
  • if a=0a = 0a=0, the number bibibi is called purely imaginary (for example 23i23i23i, −i-i−i, i2i\sqrt 2i2​).

Note · When two complex numbers are equal

a+bi=c+dia + bi = c + dia+bi=c+di exactly when a=ca = ca=c and b=db = db=d. In the handouts this is implicit in the way a complex number is written, and it becomes evident in section 2.D: each a+bia + bia+bi corresponds to a single point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) of the plane, and two points coincide when they have the same coordinates. For example x+yi=3−2ix + yi = 3 - 2ix+yi=3−2i, with x,yx, yx,y real, means x=3x = 3x=3 and y=−2y = -2y=−2. An equality between complex numbers is therefore equivalent to two equalities between real numbers: it is the trick for solving many equations (exercises 6 and 7).

Pitfall · The imaginary part does not contain iii

Shortly the number bbb will be called the imaginary part of a+bia + bia+bi. It is the real number bbb, not bibibi: the imaginary part of 4−i4 - i4−i is −1-1−1, not −i-i−i.

§3

Sum and product

p. 6

The handouts say that complex numbers are added and multiplied "in the usual way", keeping in mind a single new relation:

i2=−1.i^2 = -1.i2=−1.

"In the usual way" means: as you do with literal expressions, treating iii as a letter (like the xxx of 3+2x3 + 2x3+2x) and using the commutative, associative and distributive properties. The only novelty is that, every time i2i^2i2 appears, you replace it with −1-1−1.

The sum

(a+bi)+(c+di)=(a+c)+(b+d)i(a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i(a+bi)+(c+di)=(a+c)+(b+d)i

You add the parts without iii together and the parts with iii together, exactly as (3+2x)+(1−5x)=4−3x(3 + 2x) + (1 - 5x) = 4 - 3x(3+2x)+(1−5x)=4−3x.

Example · Sum and difference

(3+2i)+(1−5i)=(3+1)+(2−5)i=4−3i.(3 + 2i) + (1 - 5i) = (3 + 1) + (2 - 5)i = 4 - 3i.(3+2i)+(1−5i)=(3+1)+(2−5)i=4−3i.

The difference is done in the same way, taking care that the minus sign changes both parts of the second number:

(3+2i)−(1−5i)=(3−1)+(2+5)i=2+7i.(3 + 2i) - (1 - 5i) = (3 - 1) + (2 + 5)i = 2 + 7i.(3+2i)−(1−5i)=(3−1)+(2+5)i=2+7i.

The product

To multiply (a+bi)(a + bi)(a+bi) by (c+di)(c + di)(c+di) you proceed like this.

  1. Distributive property: each term of the first bracket times each term of the second,
    (a+bi)(c+di)=ac+a⋅di+bi⋅c+bi⋅di.(a + bi)(c + di) = ac + a \cdot di + bi \cdot c + bi \cdot di.(a+bi)(c+di)=ac+a⋅di+bi⋅c+bi⋅di.
  2. Reorder the factors: ac+adi+bci+bd i2ac + adi + bci + bd\,i^2ac+adi+bci+bdi2.
  3. Use the new rule: bd i2=bd⋅(−1)=−bdbd\,i^2 = bd \cdot (-1) = -bdbdi2=bd⋅(−1)=−bd.
  4. Collect the parts without iii and those with iii:
    (a+bi)⋅(c+di)=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i.(a + bi) \cdot (c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i.(a+bi)⋅(c+di)=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i.

In the product a minus sign appears (ac−bdac - bdac−bd) that is not there in the sum: it all comes from i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1.

Example · The handouts' product: (7+i)(4−i)=29−3i(7 + i)(4 - i) = 29 - 3i(7+i)(4−i)=29−3i

The four products:

  • 7⋅4=287 \cdot 4 = 287⋅4=28;
  • 7⋅(−i)=−7i7 \cdot (-i) = -7i7⋅(−i)=−7i;
  • i⋅4=4ii \cdot 4 = 4ii⋅4=4i;
  • i⋅(−i)=−i2=−(−1)=+1i \cdot (-i) = -i^2 = -(-1) = +1i⋅(−i)=−i2=−(−1)=+1.

Adding up: 28+1+(−7+4)i=29−3i28 + 1 + (-7 + 4)i = 29 - 3i28+1+(−7+4)i=29−3i. With the formula: a=7a = 7a=7, b=1b = 1b=1, c=4c = 4c=4, d=−1d = -1d=−1, so ac−bd=28−(1)(−1)=29ac - bd = 28 - (1)(-1) = 29ac−bd=28−(1)(−1)=29 and ad+bc=7⋅(−1)+1⋅4=−3ad + bc = 7 \cdot (-1) + 1 \cdot 4 = -3ad+bc=7⋅(−1)+1⋅4=−3.

The last product is a real number. It is not a coincidence: you will understand why shortly, with the conjugate.

Method · Multiplying two complex numbers

  1. Carry out the four products: each term of the first bracket times each term of the second.
  2. Replace i2i^2i2 with −1-1−1: the term bi⋅di=bd i2bi \cdot di = bd\,i^2bi⋅di=bdi2 changes sign and becomes −bd-bd−bd.
  3. Collect the parts without iii and those with iii.

There is no need to learn the formula by heart: these three steps are enough.

Pitfall · You do not multiply "part by part"

(1+2i)(3−i)(1 + 2i)(3 - i)(1+2i)(3−i) is not 1⋅3+2⋅(−1) i=3−2i1 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot (-1)\,i = 3 - 2i1⋅3+2⋅(−1)i=3−2i: the two mixed terms 1⋅(−i)1 \cdot (-i)1⋅(−i) and 2i⋅32i \cdot 32i⋅3 are missing. The right result is 5+5i5 + 5i5+5i. The second typical mistake is forgetting the change of sign: with i2=+1i^2 = +1i2=+1 you would get 3+5i−2=1+5i3 + 5i - 2 = 1 + 5i3+5i−2=1+5i, which is wrong.

The powers of iii (beyond the handouts)

The powers of iii repeat every four:

nnn000111222333444555666777888

Indeed i3=i2⋅i=−ii^3 = i^2 \cdot i = -ii3=i2⋅i=−i and i4=i2⋅i2=(−1)(−1)=1i^4 = i^2 \cdot i^2 = (-1)(-1) = 1i4=i2⋅i2=(−1)(−1)=1. From there it starts again: i5=i4⋅i=ii^5 = i^4 \cdot i = ii5=i4⋅i=i, and so on. So to compute ini^nin you only need the remainder of the division of nnn by 444: if n=4k+rn = 4k + rn=4k+r, then

in=(i4)k⋅ir=1k⋅ir=ir.i^n = (i^4)^k \cdot i^r = 1^k \cdot i^r = i^r.in=(i4)k⋅ir=1k⋅ir=ir.
  • i15i^{15}i15: 15=4⋅3+315 = 4 \cdot 3 + 315=4⋅3+3, so i15=i3=−ii^{15} = i^3 = -ii15=i3=−i (needed in exercise 2).
  • i100i^{100}i100: 100=4⋅25+0100 = 4 \cdot 25 + 0100=4⋅25+0, so i100=1i^{100} = 1i100=1.
  • i2026i^{2026}i2026: 2026=4⋅506+22026 = 4 \cdot 506 + 22026=4⋅506+2, so i2026=i2=−1i^{2026} = i^2 = -1i2026=i2=−1.

−i-i−i too has square −1-1−1: (−i)2=(−1)2⋅i2=−1(-i)^2 = (-1)^2 \cdot i^2 = -1(−i)2=(−1)2⋅i2=−1. So x2=−1x^2 = -1x2=−1 has two solutions in C\CC, iii and −i-i−i.

The set of complex numbers

The set of complex numbers is denoted by C\CC, and the chain of number sets of lesson L01 gets longer:

N⊊Z⊊Q⊊R⊊C.\N \subsetneq \Z \subsetneq \Q \subsetneq \R \subsetneq \C.N⊊Z⊊Q⊊R⊊C.

The inclusion R⊊C\R \subsetneq \CR⊊C is strict because i∈Ci \in \Ci∈C but i∉Ri \notin \Ri∈/R: its square is −1-1−1, and no real number has a negative square. Moreover, computations between real numbers do not change when you look at them inside C\CC: with the product formula, (a+0i)(c+0i)=(ac−0⋅0)+(a⋅0+0⋅c)i=ac(a + 0i)(c + 0i) = (ac - 0 \cdot 0) + (a \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot c)i = ac(a+0i)(c+0i)=(ac−0⋅0)+(a⋅0+0⋅c)i=ac. This is why we say that C\CC extends R\RR.

§4

The properties of C: a field that is not ordered

pp. 6–7

Proposition 2.2

With the addition and multiplication defined above, the set C\CC has the following properties:

  1. there is an identity element 000 for addition +++, such that 0+a=a+0=a0 + a = a + 0 = a0+a=a+0=a, ∀a∈C\forall a \in \C∀a∈C;
  2. the commutative property holds a+b=b+aa + b = b + aa+b=b+a, ∀a,b∈C\forall a, b \in \C∀a,b∈C;
  3. the associative property holds a+(b+c)=(a+b)+ca + (b + c) = (a + b) + ca+(b+c)=(a+b)+c, ∀a,b,c∈C\forall a, b, c \in \C∀a,b,c∈C;
  4. every element a∈Ca \in \Ca∈C has an inverse (or opposite) −a-a−a, such that a+(−a)=(−a)+a=0a + (-a) = (-a) + a = 0a+(−a)=(−a)+a=0;
  5. there is an identity element 111 for multiplication, such that 1⋅a=a⋅1=a1 \cdot a = a \cdot 1 = a1⋅a=a⋅1=a, ∀a∈C\forall a \in \C∀a∈C;
  6. the commutative property holds a⋅b=b⋅aa \cdot b = b \cdot aa⋅b=b⋅a, ∀a,b∈C\forall a, b \in \C∀a,b∈C;
  7. the associative property holds a⋅(b⋅c)=(a⋅b)⋅ca \cdot (b \cdot c) = (a \cdot b) \cdot ca⋅(b⋅c)=(a⋅b)⋅c, ∀a,b,c∈C\forall a, b, c \in \C∀a,b,c∈C;
  8. every element a∈Ca \in \Ca∈C with a≠0a \neq 0a=0 has an inverse a−1a^{-1}a−1, such that a⋅a−1=a−1⋅a=1a \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} \cdot a = 1a⋅a−1=a−1⋅a=1;
  9. the distributive property holds a⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅ca \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot ca⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅c, ∀a,b,c∈C\forall a, b, c \in \C∀a,b,c∈C.

They are the same nine properties as Proposition 1.5 for R\RR (lesson L01). Watch out for the letters: here a,b,ca, b, ca,b,c denote complex numbers, not the components of a+bia + bia+bi. In C\CC:

  • zero is 0=0+0i0 = 0 + 0i0=0+0i and one is 1=1+0i1 = 1 + 0i1=1+0i;
  • the opposite of a+bia + bia+bi is −a−bi-a - bi−a−bi, because (a+bi)+(−a−bi)=0+0i=0(a + bi) + (-a - bi) = 0 + 0i = 0(a+bi)+(−a−bi)=0+0i=0;
  • the only property that requires a real computation is 8, the inverse: you will see it in the section on the inverse.

The handouts conclude: "So, like R\RR, C\CC is also a field." From this lesson on, when the course says "a field K\KK", it will almost always mean K=R\K = \RK=R or K=C\K = \CK=C (lesson L05).

Beyond the handouts · what you gain

Since the nine properties hold, all the computation rules valid in R\RR work in C\CC: special products like (z+w)2=z2+2zw+w2(z + w)^2 = z^2 + 2zw + w^2(z+w)2=z2+2zw+w2 and (z−w)(z+w)=z2−w2(z - w)(z + w) = z^2 - w^2(z−w)(z+w)=z2−w2, factoring out, the zero-product rule (if zw=0zw = 0zw=0 and z≠0z \neq 0z=0, multiplying by z−1z^{-1}z−1 you get w=0w = 0w=0). You will use it in lesson L04 to find the roots of polynomials.

C is not ordered

The handouts stress a fundamental difference between C\CC and all the number sets seen before (N\NN, Z\ZZ, Q\QQ and R\RR): C\CC is not ordered. There is no notion of greater and smaller between complex numbers. The reason, in one line from the handouts: in an ordered field a square is always positive, but here i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1.

Proof · why C\CC cannot be ordered

In an ordered field like R\RR (lesson L01: a>ba > ba>b means a−b>0a - b > 0a−b>0) the positive numbers obey two rules:

  1. sum and product of positive numbers are positive;
  2. for every a≠0a \neq 0a=0, one and only one of aaa and −a-a−a is positive.

From these two rules it follows that the square of a non-zero number is positive: if a>0a > 0a>0, then a⋅a>0a \cdot a > 0a⋅a>0 by rule 1; if instead a<0a < 0a<0, then −a>0-a > 0−a>0 and a2=(−a)⋅(−a)>0a^2 = (-a) \cdot (-a) > 0a2=(−a)⋅(−a)>0, again by rule 1.

Suppose by contradiction that C\CC has an order with these rules. Then 1=121 = 1^21=12 is positive, because it is the square of 1≠01 \neq 01=0. But −1=i2-1 = i^2−1=i2 is positive too, because it is the square of i≠0i \neq 0i=0. So 111 and −1-1−1 would both be positive, against rule 2. Contradiction.

(Complex numbers can also be lined up in some way, for example first by real part and then by imaginary part; but no order of this kind respects the rules of computation. It is in this sense that C\CC is not ordered.)

Pitfall · No inequalities between complex numbers

Expressions like z>0z > 0z>0, 3i>2i3i > 2i3i>2i or 1+i<21 + i < 21+i<2 make no sense. You can only compare real numbers linked to zzz, like the real part, the imaginary part or the modulus: ∣3i∣=3>2=∣2i∣|3i| = 3 > 2 = |2i|∣3i∣=3>2=∣2i∣ is perfectly fine.

§5

Real part, imaginary part and conjugate

p. 7

Definition · Real part and imaginary part (p. 7)

Let z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi be a complex number. The numbers aaa and bbb are called respectively the real part and the imaginary part of zzz. We write a=Re⁡(z)a = \operatorname{Re}(z)a=Re(z) and b=Im⁡(z)b = \operatorname{Im}(z)b=Im(z). The number zzz is real, that is it belongs to the subset R⊂C\R \subset \CR⊂C, if and only if its imaginary part is zero.

Definition · Conjugate (p. 7)

The conjugate of z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi is the complex number

zˉ=a−bi\bar z = a - bizˉ=a−bi

obtained from zzz by changing the sign of its imaginary part.

Piece by piece:

  • Re⁡(z)\operatorname{Re}(z)Re(z) and Im⁡(z)\operatorname{Im}(z)Im(z) are two real numbers: they associate a real number with each complex number.
  • zˉ\bar zzˉ is read "z bar" (or "z conjugate"): it is written with a small bar on top. With a long expression the bar covers everything: z+w‾\overline{z + w}z+w​ is the conjugate of the sum.
  • The conjugate changes the sign only of the imaginary part: the real part stays as it is.

Beyond the handouts · four useful rules on the conjugate

  • z+zˉ=(a+bi)+(a−bi)=2az + \bar z = (a + bi) + (a - bi) = 2az+zˉ=(a+bi)+(a−bi)=2a: the sum of a number and its conjugate is always real, and Re⁡(z)=z+zˉ2\operatorname{Re}(z) = \frac{z + \bar z}2Re(z)=2z+zˉ​.

§6

The modulus

p. 7

Definition · Modulus (p. 7)

The modulus of z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi is the real number

∣z∣=a2+b2.|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}.∣z∣=a2+b2​.

Piece by piece:

  • a2+b2a^2 + b^2a2+b2 is a sum of squares of real numbers, so it is ≥0\ge 0≥0 and the root exists: ∣z∣|z|∣z∣ is a real, non-negative number.
  • If z=az = az=a is real, ∣a∣=a2|a| = \sqrt{a^2}∣a∣=a2​ is the usual absolute value (lesson L01: x2=∣x∣\sqrt{x^2} = |x|x2​=∣x∣). This is why the same symbol is used.
  • In the complex plane ∣z∣|z|∣z∣ is the distance of the point zzz from the origin (you see it in the section on the complex plane).

The most used formula: zzˉ=∣z∣2z\bar z = |z|^2zzˉ=∣z∣2

Let us multiply a number by its conjugate:

z⋅zˉ=(a+bi)(a−bi)=a2+b2=∣z∣2.z \cdot \bar z = (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2.z⋅zˉ=(a+bi)(a−bi)=a2+b2=∣z∣2.

And this also explains the product (1+i)(1−i)=2(1 + i)(1 - i) = 2(1+i)(1−i)=2 in the table above: it is ∣1+i∣2=(2)2|1 + i|^2 = (\sqrt 2)^2∣1+i∣2=(2​)2.

The idea · the conjugate "makes the iii disappear"

Whatever zzz is, the product zzˉz\bar zzzˉ is a real and non-negative number. Multiplying by the conjugate is the way to turn a complex number into a real number: the inverse and the division are based on this.

Pitfall · ∣z∣2|z|^2∣z∣2 is not z2z^2z2

∣z∣2=a2+b2|z|^2 = a^2 + b^2∣z∣2=a2+b2 is always real; z2=a2−b2+2abiz^2 = a^2 - b^2 + 2abiz2=a2−b2+2abi in general is not. With z=iz = iz=i: ∣i∣2=1|i|^2 = 1∣i∣2=1 but i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1. With z=1+iz = 1 + iz=1+i: ∣z∣2=2|z|^2 = 2∣z∣2=2 but z2=2iz^2 = 2iz2=2i. And the modulus is not the sum of the parts: ∣3+4i∣=5|3 + 4i| = 5∣3+4i∣=5, not 3+4=73 + 4 = 73+4=7.

§7

The inverse and division

pp. 7–8

Property 8 of Proposition 2.2 promises that every z≠0z \neq 0z=0 has an inverse. The handouts show it with an explicit formula: it is an important fact, because at first sight it is not clear how to write 12+i\frac 1{2 + i}2+i1​ in the form c+dic + dic+di.

Proposition · Inverse of a complex number (p. 7)

As in the rational and real numbers, every complex number z≠0z \neq 0z=0 has an inverse z−1z^{-1}z−1 with respect to the multiplication operation, given by

z−1=zˉ∣z∣2.z^{-1} = \frac{\bar z}{|z|^2}.z−1=∣z∣2zˉ​.

Piece by piece:

  • ∣z∣2=a2+b2|z|^2 = a^2 + b^2∣z∣2=a2+b2 is a real, non-zero number (because z≠0z \neq 0z=0): dividing by it means multiplying the two parts of zˉ\bar zzˉ by the real number 1a2+b2\frac 1{a^2 + b^2}a2+b21​.
  • In coordinates:
    (a+bi)−1=a−bia2+b2=aa2+b2−ba2+b2 i.(a + bi)^{-1} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2} = \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} - \frac{b}{a^2 + b^2}\,i.(a+bi)−1=a2+b2a−bi​=a2+b2a​−a2+b2b​i.
  • Instead of z−1z^{-1}z−1 one also writes 1z\frac 1zz1​.

Why it works (it is the handouts' check). Let us multiply zzz by the candidate inverse and use zzˉ=∣z∣2z\bar z = |z|^2zzˉ=∣z∣2:

z⋅z−1=zzˉ∣z∣2=∣z∣2∣z∣2=1.z \cdot z^{-1} = \frac{z \bar z}{|z|^2} = \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2} = 1.z⋅z−1=∣z∣2zzˉ​=∣z∣2∣z∣2​=1.

By the commutative property, z−1⋅z=1z^{-1} \cdot z = 1z−1⋅z=1 holds as well.

The idea · where the formula comes from

To write 1a+bi\frac 1{a + bi}a+bi1​ in the form c+dic + dic+di you need to remove the iii from the denominator. It is done as with roots in lesson L01 (for 12−1\frac 1{\sqrt 2 - 1}2​−11​ you multiplied top and bottom by 2+1\sqrt 2 + 12​+1): you multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator,

1a+bi=a−bi(a+bi)(a−bi)=a−bia2+b2.\frac 1{a + bi} = \frac{a - bi}{(a + bi)(a - bi)} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2}.a+bi1​=(a+bi)(a−bi)a−bi​=a2+b2a−bi​.

Example 2.3 · The inverses of iii and of 2+i2 + i2+i

The inverse of iii is −i-i−i: indeed i⋅(−i)=−i2=1i \cdot (-i) = -i^2 = 1i⋅(−i)=−i2=1. With the formula: iˉ=−i\bar i = -iiˉ=−i and ∣i∣2=1|i|^2 = 1∣i∣2=1, so i−1=−ii^{-1} = -ii−1=−i.

The inverse of 2+i2 + i2+i is

(2+i)−1=2−i∣2+i∣2=2−i5=25−15i,(2 + i)^{-1} = \frac{2 - i}{|2 + i|^2} = \frac{2 - i}5 = \frac 25 - \frac 15 i,(2+i)−1=∣2+i∣22−i​=52−i​=52​−51​i,

because ∣2+i∣2=4+1=5|2 + i|^2 = 4 + 1 = 5∣2+i∣2=4+1=5. You can check that indeed

(2+i)⋅2−i5=4−2i+2i−i25=4+15=1.(2 + i) \cdot \frac{2 - i}5 = \frac{4 - 2i + 2i - i^2}5 = \frac{4 + 1}5 = 1.(2+i)⋅52−i​=54−2i+2i−i2​=54+1​=1.

Two more examples with the same pattern:

  • (3+4i)−1=3−4i25=325−425i(3 + 4i)^{-1} = \frac{3 - 4i}{25} = \frac 3{25} - \frac 4{25}i(3+4i)−1=253−4i​=253​−254​i, because ∣3+4i∣2=25|3 + 4i|^2 = 25∣3+4i∣2=25;
  • (1−i)−1=1+i2=12+12i(1 - i)^{-1} = \frac{1 + i}{2} = \frac 12 + \frac 12 i(1−i)−1=21+i​=21​+21​i, because ∣1−i∣2=2|1 - i|^2 = 2∣1−i∣2=2.

Dividing two complex numbers

Dividing by z≠0z \neq 0z=0 means multiplying by its inverse: wz=w⋅z−1=wzˉ∣z∣2\frac wz = w \cdot z^{-1} = \frac{w\bar z}{|z|^2}zw​=w⋅z−1=∣z∣2wzˉ​. In practice:

Method · Dividing two complex numbers

  1. Write the fraction wz\frac wzzw​.
  2. Multiply numerator and denominator by zˉ\bar zzˉ, the conjugate of the denominator.
  3. In the denominator you get zzˉ=∣z∣2z\bar z = |z|^2zzˉ=∣z∣2, a positive real number; in the numerator carry out the product wzˉw\bar zwzˉ.
  4. Divide the real part and the imaginary part of the numerator by ∣z∣2|z|^2∣z∣2.
  5. Check: multiply the result by zzz; you must get www back.

Example · 4+3i1+2i\frac{4 + 3i}{1 + 2i}1+2i4+3i​

The conjugate of the denominator is 1−2i1 - 2i1−2i:

4+3i1+2i=(4+3i)(1−2i)(1+2i)(1−2i)=4−8i+3i−6i21+4=10−5i5=2−i.\frac{4 + 3i}{1 + 2i} = \frac{(4 + 3i)(1 - 2i)}{(1 + 2i)(1 - 2i)} = \frac{4 - 8i + 3i - 6i^2}{1 + 4} = \frac{10 - 5i}5 = 2 - i.1+2i4+3i​=(1+2i)(1−2i)(4+3i)(1−2i)​=1+44−8i+3i−6i2​=510−5i​=2−i.

Check: (2−i)(1+2i)=2+4i−i−2i2=4+3i(2 - i)(1 + 2i) = 2 + 4i - i - 2i^2 = 4 + 3i(2−i)(1+2i)=2+4i−i−2i2=4+3i. Correct.

Example · 1+i1−i\frac{1 + i}{1 - i}1−i1+i​

1+i1−i=(1+i)(1+i)(1−i)(1+i)=1+2i+i22=2i2=i.\frac{1 + i}{1 - i} = \frac{(1 + i)(1 + i)}{(1 - i)(1 + i)} = \frac{1 + 2i + i^2}{2} = \frac{2i}2 = i.1−i1+i​=(1−i)(1+i)(1+i)(1+i)​=21+2i+i2​=22i​=i.

Check: i(1−i)=i−i2=1+ii(1 - i) = i - i^2 = 1 + ii(1−i)=i−i2=1+i.

Pitfall · You do not divide "part by part"

4+3i1+2i\frac{4 + 3i}{1 + 2i}1+2i4+3i​ is not 41+32i\frac 41 + \frac 32 i14​+23​i. Check: (1+2i)(4+32i)=4+32i+8i+3i2=1+192i(1 + 2i)(4 + \frac 32 i) = 4 + \frac 32 i + 8i + 3i^2 = 1 + \frac{19}2 i(1+2i)(4+23​i)=4+23​i+8i+3i2=1+219​i, which is not 4+3i4 + 3i4+3i. You can divide part by part only by a real number: this is why you first bring the real number ∣z∣2|z|^2∣z∣2 into the denominator.

First-degree equations in C

An equation like (1+2i)z=4+3i(1 + 2i)z = 4 + 3i(1+2i)z=4+3i is solved as among the reals: you divide by the coefficient of zzz, which is not zero. So z=4+3i1+2i=2−iz = \frac{4 + 3i}{1 + 2i} = 2 - iz=1+2i4+3i​=2−i, the quotient just computed.

Matters in the exam · The most direct kind of question

"Find zzz such that (…)z=…(\ldots)z = \ldots(…)z=…" was question 1 of the quiz in the exam sessions of 08/02/2024, 03/06/2025 and 03/06/2026. The method is always this: simplify the products, divide with the conjugate, check by multiplying. The three questions, solved, are in the section "Towards the exam".

§8

The complex plane

pp. 8–9

While the real numbers R\RR form a line, the complex numbers C\CC form a plane, called the complex plane. Each complex number a+bia + bia+bi is identified with the point with coordinates (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) of the Cartesian plane, or, equivalently, with the vector applied at the origin 000 and pointing to (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) (Figure 1 of the handouts).

  • The horizontal axis is the real axis: it is exactly the subset R⊂C\R \subset \CR⊂C of the real numbers.
  • The vertical axis is the imaginary axis: it contains all the numbers of the form bibibi, as b∈Rb \in \Rb∈R varies.

The number −3-3−3 lies on the real axis and 2i2i2i on the imaginary axis. The number 2+i2 + i2+i is drawn as an arrow: it is the vector that starts at the origin and ends at the point (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1).

The modulus is a distance

The modulus ∣a+bi∣=a2+b2|a + bi| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}∣a+bi∣=a2+b2​ is the length of the vector, that is the distance of the point from the origin: by Pythagoras' theorem, in the right triangle with legs of length ∣a∣|a|∣a∣ and ∣b∣|b|∣b∣ the hypotenuse has length a2+b2\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}a2+b2​. The handouts note it in lesson L03, when they introduce polar coordinates.

Conjugate and opposite

In the plane, the conjugate zˉ=a−bi\bar z = a - bizˉ=a−bi has the same abscissa and the ordinate with its sign changed: it is the mirror image of zzz with respect to the real axis (the handouts say this too, in lesson L03). The opposite −z=−a−bi-z = -a - bi−z=−a−bi is instead the mirror image with respect to the origin.

The sum: the parallelogram rule

The sum z1+z2z_1 + z_2z1​+z2​ is computed by interpreting z1z_1z1​ and z2z_2z2​ as vectors and adding them with the parallelogram rule: the point z1+z2z_1 + z_2z1​+z2​ is the fourth vertex of the parallelogram that has three vertices at 000, z1z_1z1​ and z2z_2z2​. It works because the sum is done coordinate by coordinate, exactly like the sum of vectors in the plane (you will meet it again in lesson L05).

Read the drawing like this: start from 000, go to z1z_1z1​ and from there make the same move that takes 000 to z2z_2z2​ (444 to the right and 111 up): you arrive at 5+4i5 + 4i5+4i. Or do z2z_2z2​ first and then z1z_1z1​: you arrive at the same point, because the sum is commutative.

Beyond the handouts · the difference and the distance between two points

The difference z−wz - wz−w is the vector that goes from www to zzz. Its modulus is the distance between the two points: with z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi and w=c+diw = c + diw=c+di,

∣z−w∣=(a−c)2+(b−d)2,|z - w| = \sqrt{(a - c)^2 + (b - d)^2},∣z−w∣=(a−c)2+(b−d)2​,

which is the distance formula of analytic geometry. For example the distance between 1+i1 + i1+i and 4+5i4 + 5i4+5i is ∣3+4i∣=5|3 + 4i| = 5∣3+4i∣=5. Consequently {z∈C∣∣z−c∣=r}\{z \in \C \mid |z - c| = r\}{z∈C∣∣z−c∣=r} is the circle with centre ccc and radius rrr: it is needed in exercise 4.

And the product?

The product z1⋅z2z_1 \cdot z_2z1​⋅z2​ also has a geometric meaning, which can be seen clearly only with polar coordinates: you study it in lesson L03. A foretaste: multiplying by iii rotates the point by a right angle anticlockwise. For example i(2+i)=2i+i2=−1+2ii(2 + i) = 2i + i^2 = -1 + 2ii(2+i)=2i+i2=−1+2i, and i(−1+2i)=−i+2i2=−2−ii(-1 + 2i) = -i + 2i^2 = -2 - ii(−1+2i)=−i+2i2=−2−i.

Try it yourself with the tool below. In z + w mode drag the points zzz and www: the parallelogram updates and below it you read the coordinates of the sum. Then choose conjugate and inverse of z: you see zˉ\bar zzˉ mirrored with respect to the real axis and 1/z1/z1/z, which lies inside the unit circle when ∣z∣>1|z| > 1∣z∣>1 and outside when ∣z∣<1|z| < 1∣z∣<1 (you will understand why in lesson L03).

§9

Drawing sets of complex numbers

beyond the handouts

Exercise 2.6 of the handouts asks you to draw sets of complex numbers defined by a condition. The method is always the same.

Method · From a condition on zzz to a drawing

  1. Write z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi with x,yx, yx,y real: Re⁡(z)=x\operatorname{Re}(z) = xRe(z)=x, Im⁡(z)=y\operatorname{Im}(z) = yIm(z)=y, zˉ=x−yi\bar z = x - yizˉ=x−yi, ∣z∣=x2+y2|z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}∣z∣=x2+y2​.
  2. Translate the condition into a condition on xxx and yyy. If it is an equality between complex numbers, equate real parts and imaginary parts.
  3. Recognise the figure: line, half-plane, circle, disc. Remember that ∣z−c∣|z - c|∣z−c∣ is the distance of zzz from the point ccc.
ConditionIn xxx and yyyFigure
Re⁡(z)=2\operatorname{Re}(z) = 2Re(z)=2x=2x = 2x=2vertical line
Im⁡(z)>1\operatorname{Im}(z) > 1Im(z)>1y>1y > 1y>1half-plane above the line y=1y = 1y=1, line excluded
∣z∣=3\lvert z \rvert = 3∣z∣=3x2+y2=9x^2 + y^2 = 9x2+y2=9circle with centre 000 and radius 333

Let us check the last row, which cannot be guessed by eye. ∣z−1∣|z - 1|∣z−1∣ is the distance from 111 and ∣z+1∣=∣z−(−1)∣|z + 1| = |z - (-1)|∣z+1∣=∣z−(−1)∣ is the distance from −1-1−1: the points equidistant from 111 and from −1-1−1 form the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, that is the imaginary axis. With the computations: squaring, (x−1)2+y2=(x+1)2+y2(x - 1)^2 + y^2 = (x + 1)^2 + y^2(x−1)2+y2=(x+1)2+y2, that is x2−2x+1=x2+2x+1x^2 - 2x + 1 = x^2 + 2x + 1x2−2x+1=x2+2x+1, that is −4x=0-4x = 0−4x=0, that is x=0x = 0x=0.

Beyond the handouts · where to find it in the book

In Martelli's book this lesson corresponds to §1.4, parts 1.4.1 "Definizione", 1.4.2 "Coniugio, norma e inverso" (with Example 1.4.1, which is 2.3 in the handouts) and 1.4.3 "Il piano complesso", on pp. 25–27 of the book. Exercise 1.4.3 (p. 30) lists the properties of the modulus and of the conjugate, including those of exercise 2.5 of the handouts; §1.5.3 (p. 36) defines fields in general.

§10

Towards the exam

exam

The test in two lines. 10 multiple-choice questions (5 answers, one right) and 2 problems worth 11 points, marked only with at least 6 points in the quiz; 2 hours, no calculator, only 4 handwritten pages of notes. 2026/27 Linear Algebra exam sessions: 22/01/2027 and 05/02/2027 at 14:00. Complete rules and sources in lesson L01.

Complex numbers in the exam sessions. In each of the 15 exam sessions from 24/01/2024 to 07/09/2026 there is at least one quiz question on complex numbers or on the roots of a polynomial, and in 11 sessions out of 15 it is question 1. They split like this among lessons L02–L04:

Type of questionExam sessions (question)Lesson
find zzz from a first-degree equation, then compute an expression08/02/2024 (1), 03/06/2025 (1), 03/06/2026 (1)L02
high powers, product in polar form, nnn-th roots24/01/2024 (2), 10/06/2024 (1), 10/07/2024 (1), 06/09/2024 (1), 16/01/2025 (1), 07/02/2025 (1), 02/09/2025 (2), 15/01/2026 (5), 05/02/2026 (1)L03
which number is a root of a polynomial10/07/2025 (1), 03/07/2026 (7), 07/09/2026 (1)L04

The questions of lessons L03 and L04 too almost always end with the computations of this lesson: a product, an inverse, a division. Here are the three questions of type L02, with the solution.

Example · Exam of 08/02/2024, question 1

Find z∈Cz \in \Cz∈C such that (i−1)(i−2)z=(i+1)(i+2)(i+3)(i - 1)(i - 2)z = (i + 1)(i + 2)(i + 3)(i−1)(i−2)z=(i+1)(i+2)(i+3). Answers: 10+3i10 + 3i10+3i; i−3i - 3i−3; 30+10i30 + 10i30+10i; 3i−13i - 13i−1; 1−30i1 - 30i1−30i.

Solution. First simplify the two sides.

  • (i−1)(i−2)=i2−2i−i+2=−1−3i+2=1−3i(i - 1)(i - 2) = i^2 - 2i - i + 2 = -1 - 3i + 2 = 1 - 3i(i−1)(i−2)=i2−2i−i+2=−1−3i+2=1−3i.
  • (i+1)(i+2)=i2+3i+2=1+3i(i + 1)(i + 2) = i^2 + 3i + 2 = 1 + 3i(i+1)(i+2)=i2+3i+2=1+3i, and then (1+3i)(i+3)=i+3+3i2+9i=3−3+10i=10i(1 + 3i)(i + 3) = i + 3 + 3i^2 + 9i = 3 - 3 + 10i = 10i(1+3i)(i+3)=i+3+3i2+9i=3−3+10i=10i.

The equation becomes (1−3i)z=10i(1 - 3i)z = 10i(1−3i)z=10i, so

z=10i1−3i=10i(1+3i)(1−3i)(1+3i)=10i+30i210=−30+10i10=−3+i.z = \frac{10i}{1 - 3i} = \frac{10i(1 + 3i)}{(1 - 3i)(1 + 3i)} = \frac{10i + 30i^2}{10} = \frac{-30 + 10i}{10} = -3 + i.z=1−3i10i​=(1−3i)(1+3i)10i(1+3i)​=1010i+30i2​=10−30+10i​=−3+i.

It is the answer i−3i - 3i−3. Check: (1−3i)(−3+i)=−3+i+9i−3i2=−3+10i+3=10i(1 - 3i)(-3 + i) = -3 + i + 9i - 3i^2 = -3 + 10i + 3 = 10i(1−3i)(−3+i)=−3+i+9i−3i2=−3+10i+3=10i.

Example · Exam of 03/06/2025, question 1

Given z∈Cz \in \Cz∈C satisfying (1+i)z=3+2i(1 + i)z = 3 + 2i(1+i)z=3+2i, what is 2z(5+i)2z(5 + i)2z(5+i)? Answers: 13+13i13 + 13i13+13i; 26i26i26i; 1+i1 + i1+i; 13−13i13 - 13i13−13i; 262626.

Solution. z=3+2i1+i=(3+2i)(1−i)2=3−3i+2i−2i22=5−i2z = \frac{3 + 2i}{1 + i} = \frac{(3 + 2i)(1 - i)}{2} = \frac{3 - 3i + 2i - 2i^2}2 = \frac{5 - i}2z=1+i3+2i​=2(3+2i)(1−i)​=23−3i+2i−2i2​=25−i​. Then

2z(5+i)=(5−i)(5+i)=25−i2=26.2z(5 + i) = (5 - i)(5 + i) = 25 - i^2 = 26.2z(5+i)=(5−i)(5+i)=25−i2=26.

The product is real because 5−i5 - i5−i and 5+i5 + i5+i are conjugates: (5−i)(5+i)=∣5+i∣2=25+1(5 - i)(5 + i) = |5 + i|^2 = 25 + 1(5−i)(5+i)=∣5+i∣2=25+1. Answer: 262626.

Example · Exam of 03/06/2026, question 1

If (1+i)z=2i(1 + i)z = 2i(1+i)z=2i, what is 1z+i\frac 1{z + i}z+i1​? Answers: 000; 11+i\frac 1{1 + i}1+i1​; 1−2i5\frac{1 - 2i}551−2i​; i1+i\frac i{1 + i}1+ii​; 2+i5\frac{2 + i}552+i​.

Solution. z=2i1+i=2i(1−i)2=i−i2=1+iz = \frac{2i}{1 + i} = \frac{2i(1 - i)}{2} = i - i^2 = 1 + iz=1+i2i​=22i(1−i)​=i−i2=1+i. So z+i=1+2iz + i = 1 + 2iz+i=1+2i and

11+2i=1−2i(1+2i)(1−2i)=1−2i5.\frac 1{1 + 2i} = \frac{1 - 2i}{(1 + 2i)(1 - 2i)} = \frac{1 - 2i}{5}.1+2i1​=(1+2i)(1−2i)1−2i​=51−2i​.

Answer: 1−2i5\frac{1 - 2i}551−2i​. Watch out for answers written in different forms: 11+i=1−i2\frac 1{1 + i} = \frac{1 - i}21+i1​=21−i​ and i1+i=1+i2\frac i{1 + i} = \frac{1 + i}21+ii​=21+i​ are numbers different from the right one, and it is always best to reduce everything to the form a+bia + bia+bi before comparing.

Method · The "find zzz" questions in five steps

  1. Carry out the products of known numbers, so that the equation becomes αz=β\alpha z = \betaαz=β with α,β\alpha, \betaα,β numbers.
  2. Divide: z=βαz = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}z=αβ​, multiplying top and bottom by αˉ\bar\alphaαˉ.
  3. Check by multiplying: α⋅z\alpha \cdot zα⋅z must give β\betaβ.
  4. Compute the required expression (sum, product, inverse).
  5. Reduce the five answers to the form a+bia + bia+bi before choosing. In the quiz you can also substitute the answers into the equation: with one product per answer you find the right one.

Mistakes to avoid. Forgetting that i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1 changes the sign; multiplying by the conjugate of the numerator instead of the denominator; confusing ∣z∣2|z|^2∣z∣2 with z2z^2z2; dividing part by part; writing inequalities between complex numbers.

Matters in the exam · The 4-page sheet

From this lesson a few lines are enough: i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1 and the powers of iii with period 4; (a+bi)(c+di)=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i(a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i(a+bi)(c+di)=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i; zˉ=a−bi\bar z = a - bizˉ=a−bi, ∣z∣=a2+b2|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}∣z∣=a2+b2​, zzˉ=∣z∣2z\bar z = |z|^2zzˉ=∣z∣2; z−1=zˉ∣z∣2z^{-1} = \frac{\bar z}{|z|^2}z−1=∣z∣2zˉ​; "to divide, I multiply by the conjugate of the denominator"; ∣z−c∣|z - c|∣z−c∣ is the distance from ccc.

Exercises

with solutions

1 · Computations with the form a+bia + bia+bi basic

Compute and write in the form a+bia + bia+bi: (a) (3−2i)+(−1+5i)(3 - 2i) + (-1 + 5i)(3−2i)+(−1+5i); (b) (3−2i)−(−1+5i)(3 - 2i) - (-1 + 5i)(3−2i)−(−1+5i); (c) (3−2i)(−1+5i)(3 - 2i)(-1 + 5i)(3−2i)(−1+5i); (d) (1−2i)2(1 - 2i)^2(1−2i)2; (e) (2+i)3(2 + i)^3(2+i)3 and (2−i)3(2 - i)^3(2−i)3 (they are the cubes of Bombelli's story).

Solution

(a) Real parts and imaginary parts separately: (3−1)+(−2+5)i=2+3i(3 - 1) + (-2 + 5)i = 2 + 3i(3−1)+(−2+5)i=2+3i.

(b) The minus changes both parts of −1+5i-1 + 5i−1+5i: (3+1)+(−2−5)i=4−7i(3 + 1) + (-2 - 5)i = 4 - 7i(3+1)+(−2−5)i=4−7i.

(c) Four products: 3⋅(−1)=−33 \cdot (-1) = -33⋅(−1)=−3; 3⋅5i=15i3 \cdot 5i = 15i3⋅5i=15i; −2i⋅(−1)=2i-2i \cdot (-1) = 2i−2i⋅(−1)=2i; −2i⋅5i=−10i2=10-2i \cdot 5i = -10i^2 = 10−2i⋅5i=−10i2=10. Sum: (−3+10)+(15+2)i=7+17i(-3 + 10) + (15 + 2)i = 7 + 17i(−3+10)+(15+2)i=7+17i.

(d) Square of a binomial: (1−2i)2=1−4i+4i2=1−4i−4=−3−4i(1 - 2i)^2 = 1 - 4i + 4i^2 = 1 - 4i - 4 = -3 - 4i(1−2i)2=1−4i+4i2=1−4i−4=−3−4i.

(e) First the square: (2+i)2=4+4i+i2=3+4i(2 + i)^2 = 4 + 4i + i^2 = 3 + 4i(2+i)2=4+4i+i2=3+4i. Then (2+i)3=(3+4i)(2+i)=6+3i+8i+4i2=2+11i(2 + i)^3 = (3 + 4i)(2 + i) = 6 + 3i + 8i + 4i^2 = 2 + 11i(2+i)3=(3+4i)(2+i)=6+3i+8i+4i2=2+11i. In the same way (2−i)2=3−4i(2 - i)^2 = 3 - 4i(2−i)2=3−4i and (2−i)3=(3−4i)(2−i)=6−3i−8i+4i2=2−11i(2 - i)^3 = (3 - 4i)(2 - i) = 6 - 3i - 8i + 4i^2 = 2 - 11i(2−i)3=(3−4i)(2−i)=6−3i−8i+4i2=2−11i. The two bases added together give (2+i)+(2−i)=4(2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4(2+i)+(2−i)=4: the real solution of x3=15x+4x^3 = 15x + 4x3=15x+4 found by Bombelli.

2 · Exercise 2.4 of the handouts: real part and imaginary part intermediate

Compute the real part and the imaginary part of the following complex numbers:

6+5i3−i,(2+i)35i15,3−2i1+5i+2−3i2−i.\frac{6 + 5i}{3 - i}, \qquad \frac{(2 + i)^3}{5i^{15}}, \qquad \frac{3 - 2i}{1 + 5i} + \frac{2 - 3i}{2 - i}.3−i6+5i​,5i15(2+i)3​,1+5i3−2i​+2−i2−3i​.
Solution

First number. I multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, 3+i3 + i3+i; in the denominator ∣3−i∣2=9+1=10|3 - i|^2 = 9 + 1 = 10∣3−i∣2=9+1=10:

6+5i3−i=(6+5i)(3+i)10=18+6i+15i+5i210=13+21i10.\frac{6 + 5i}{3 - i} = \frac{(6 + 5i)(3 + i)}{10} = \frac{18 + 6i + 15i + 5i^2}{10} = \frac{13 + 21i}{10}.3−i6+5i​=10(6+5i)(3+i)​=1018+6i+15i+5i2​=1013+21i​.

Real part 1310\frac{13}{10}1013​, imaginary part 2110\frac{21}{10}1021​.

Second number. You computed the numerator in exercise 1: (2+i)3=2+11i(2 + i)^3 = 2 + 11i(2+i)3=2+11i. In the denominator i15=i3=−ii^{15} = i^3 = -ii15=i3=−i (because 15=4⋅3+315 = 4 \cdot 3 + 315=4⋅3+3), so 5i15=−5i5i^{15} = -5i5i15=−5i. Then

2+11i−5i=(2+11i)⋅i−5i⋅i=2i+11i2−5i2=−11+2i5.\frac{2 + 11i}{-5i} = \frac{(2 + 11i) \cdot i}{-5i \cdot i} = \frac{2i + 11i^2}{-5i^2} = \frac{-11 + 2i}{5}.−5i2+11i​=−5i⋅i(2+11i)⋅i​=−5i22i+11i2​=5−11+2i​.

Here I multiplied top and bottom by iii, which is enough because the denominator is purely imaginary: −5i⋅i=−5i2=5-5i \cdot i = -5i^2 = 5−5i⋅i=−5i2=5. Real part −115-\frac{11}5−511​, imaginary part 25\frac 2552​.

Third number. Two divisions and a sum.

  • 3−2i1+5i=(3−2i)(1−5i)1+25=3−15i−2i+10i226=−7−17i26\frac{3 - 2i}{1 + 5i} = \frac{(3 - 2i)(1 - 5i)}{1 + 25} = \frac{3 - 15i - 2i + 10i^2}{26} = \frac{-7 - 17i}{26}1+5i3−2i​=1+25(3−2i)(1−5i)​=263−15i−2i+10i2​=26−7−17i​.
  • 2−3i2−i=(2−3i)(2+i)4+1=4+2i−6i−3i25=7−4i5\frac{2 - 3i}{2 - i} = \frac{(2 - 3i)(2 + i)}{4 + 1} = \frac{4 + 2i - 6i - 3i^2}{5} = \frac{7 - 4i}52−i2−3i​=4+1(2−3i)(2+i)​=54+2i−6i−3i2​=57−4i​.
  • Sum, with common denominator 130130130:
    −7−17i26+7−4i5=5(−7−17i)+26(7−4i)130,\frac{-7 - 17i}{26} + \frac{7 - 4i}{5} = \frac{5(-7 - 17i) + 26(7 - 4i)}{130},26−7−17i​+57−4i​=1305(−7−17i)+26(7−4i)​,
    and the numerator is −35−85i+182−104i=147−189i-35 - 85i + 182 - 104i = 147 - 189i−35−85i+182−104i=147−189i. So the sum is 147−189i130\frac{147 - 189i}{130}130147−189i​.

Real part 147130\frac{147}{130}130147​, imaginary part −189130-\frac{189}{130}−130189​ (the fractions cannot be simplified: 147=3⋅72147 = 3 \cdot 7^2147=3⋅72, 189=33⋅7189 = 3^3 \cdot 7189=33⋅7 and 130=2⋅5⋅13130 = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 13130=2⋅5⋅13 have no common factors).

3 · Exercise 2.5 of the handouts: properties of modulus and conjugate intermediate

Prove that for every z,w∈Cz, w \in \Cz,w∈C the following hold:

∣zˉ∣=∣z∣,∣z−1∣=1∣z∣ (z≠0),z+w‾=zˉ+wˉ,zw‾=zˉ wˉ.|\bar z| = |z|, \qquad |z^{-1}| = \frac 1{|z|} \ (z \neq 0), \qquad \overline{z + w} = \bar z + \bar w, \qquad \overline{zw} = \bar z\,\bar w.∣zˉ∣=∣z∣,∣z−1∣=∣z∣1​ (z=0),z+w​=zˉ+wˉ,zw=zˉwˉ.
Solution

I write z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi and w=c+diw = c + diw=c+di with a,b,c,da, b, c, da,b,c,d real.

1. ∣zˉ∣=∣z∣|\bar z| = |z|∣zˉ∣=∣z∣. zˉ=a+(−b)i\bar z = a + (-b)izˉ=a+(−b)i, so ∣zˉ∣=a2+(−b)2=a2+b2=∣z∣|\bar z| = \sqrt{a^2 + (-b)^2} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = |z|∣zˉ∣=a2+(−b)2​=a2+b2​=∣z∣, because (−b)2=b2(-b)^2 = b^2(−b)2=b2. In the plane: a point and its mirror image with respect to the real axis have the same distance from the origin.

2. ∣z−1∣=1∣z∣|z^{-1}| = \frac 1{|z|}∣z−1∣=∣z∣1​. For z≠0z \neq 0z=0, z−1=aa2+b2−ba2+b2 iz^{-1} = \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} - \frac{b}{a^2 + b^2}\,iz−1=a2+b2a​−a2+b2b​i. I call m=a2+b2=∣z∣2>0m = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2 > 0m=a2+b2=∣z∣2>0. Then

∣z−1∣=a2m2+b2m2=a2+b2m2=mm2=1m=1∣z∣.|z^{-1}| = \sqrt{\frac{a^2}{m^2} + \frac{b^2}{m^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{a^2 + b^2}{m^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{m}{m^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt m} = \frac 1{|z|}.∣z−1∣=m2a2​+m2b2​​=m2a2+b2​​=m2m​​=m​1​=∣z∣1​.

3. z+w‾=zˉ+wˉ\overline{z + w} = \bar z + \bar wz+w​=zˉ+wˉ. z+w=(a+c)+(b+d)iz + w = (a + c) + (b + d)iz+w=(a+c)+(b+d)i, so z+w‾=(a+c)−(b+d)i\overline{z + w} = (a + c) - (b + d)iz+w​=(a+c)−(b+d)i. On the other hand zˉ+wˉ=(a−bi)+(c−di)=(a+c)−(b+d)i\bar z + \bar w = (a - bi) + (c - di) = (a + c) - (b + d)izˉ+wˉ=(a−bi)+(c−di)=(a+c)−(b+d)i. They are equal.

4. zw‾=zˉ wˉ\overline{zw} = \bar z\,\bar wzw=zˉwˉ. From the product formula zw=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)izw = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)izw=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i, so zw‾=(ac−bd)−(ad+bc)i\overline{zw} = (ac - bd) - (ad + bc)izw=(ac−bd)−(ad+bc)i. On the other hand

zˉ wˉ=(a−bi)(c−di)=ac−adi−bci+bd i2=(ac−bd)−(ad+bc)i.\bar z\,\bar w = (a - bi)(c - di) = ac - adi - bci + bd\,i^2 = (ac - bd) - (ad + bc)i.zˉwˉ=(a−bi)(c−di)=ac−adi−bci+bdi2=(ac−bd)−(ad+bc)i.

They are equal. In words: you can conjugate before or after doing the computations. This rule will be needed in lesson L04 (Proposition 4.11).

4 · Exercise 2.6 of the handouts: three sets to draw intermediate

Draw the following subsets in the complex plane:

  1. A={z∈C such that Re⁡(z)>Im⁡(z)}A = \{z \in \C \text{ such that } \operatorname{Re}(z) > \operatorname{Im}(z)\}A={z∈C such that Re(z)>Im(z)};
  2. B={z∈C such that z+zˉ=i}B = \{z \in \C \text{ such that } z + \bar z = i\}B={z∈C such that z+zˉ=i};
  3. C={z∈C such that ∣z−2∣≥2}C = \{z \in \C \text{ such that } |z - 2| \ge 2\}C={z∈C such that ∣z−2∣≥2}.
Solution

I always write z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi.

1. The set AAA. The condition is x>yx > yx>y: the points that lie below the bisector y=xy = xy=x. It is an open half-plane: the line y=xy = xy=x is excluded, because there x=yx = yx=y holds and not x>yx > yx>y. Check with a point: z=1z = 1z=1 has x=1>0=yx = 1 > 0 = yx=1>0=y, and indeed it lies below the bisector.

2. The set BBB. z+zˉ=(x+yi)+(x−yi)=2xz + \bar z = (x + yi) + (x - yi) = 2xz+zˉ=(x+yi)+(x−yi)=2x, which is a real number. A real number cannot be equal to iii, which has imaginary part 111: equating the imaginary parts you would get 0=10 = 10=1. So B=∅B = \emptysetB=∅, the empty set: there is nothing to draw.

If the condition had been z−zˉ=iz - \bar z = iz−zˉ=i, we would have 2yi=i2yi = i2yi=i, that is y=12y = \frac 12y=21​: the horizontal line Im⁡(z)=12\operatorname{Im}(z) = \frac 12Im(z)=21​. It is always worth noticing when a condition is impossible: "the set is empty" is a complete answer, to be justified as above.

3. The set CCC. ∣z−2∣|z - 2|∣z−2∣ is the distance of zzz from the point 222. The condition asks for a distance of at least 222: these are the points outside the circle with centre 222 and radius 222, together with the circle itself. In coordinates: (x−2)2+y2≥4(x - 2)^2 + y^2 \ge 4(x−2)2+y2≥4. The open disc (x−2)2+y2<4(x - 2)^2 + y^2 < 4(x−2)2+y2<4 is excluded; the circle passes through the origin, which therefore belongs to CCC (∣0−2∣=2|0 - 2| = 2∣0−2∣=2).

5 · Inverses and quotients basic

Write in the form a+bia + bia+bi: (a) (1+i)−1(1 + i)^{-1}(1+i)−1; (b) (2−3i)−1(2 - 3i)^{-1}(2−3i)−1; (c) 5+5i1−2i\frac{5 + 5i}{1 - 2i}1−2i5+5i​; (d) i1+i\frac{i}{1 + i}1+ii​.

Solution

(a) ∣1+i∣2=2|1 + i|^2 = 2∣1+i∣2=2, so (1+i)−1=1−i2=12−12i(1 + i)^{-1} = \frac{1 - i}2 = \frac 12 - \frac 12 i(1+i)−1=21−i​=21​−21​i. Check: (1+i)(1−i)=2(1 + i)(1 - i) = 2(1+i)(1−i)=2, divided by 222 gives 111.

(b) ∣2−3i∣2=4+9=13|2 - 3i|^2 = 4 + 9 = 13∣2−3i∣2=4+9=13, so (2−3i)−1=2+3i13=213+313i(2 - 3i)^{-1} = \frac{2 + 3i}{13} = \frac 2{13} + \frac 3{13}i(2−3i)−1=132+3i​=132​+133​i.

(c) Conjugate of the denominator: 1+2i1 + 2i1+2i; ∣1−2i∣2=5|1 - 2i|^2 = 5∣1−2i∣2=5.

(5+5i)(1+2i)5=5+10i+5i+10i25=−5+15i5=−1+3i.\frac{(5 + 5i)(1 + 2i)}{5} = \frac{5 + 10i + 5i + 10i^2}{5} = \frac{-5 + 15i}5 = -1 + 3i.5(5+5i)(1+2i)​=55+10i+5i+10i2​=5−5+15i​=−1+3i.

Check: (−1+3i)(1−2i)=−1+2i+3i−6i2=5+5i(-1 + 3i)(1 - 2i) = -1 + 2i + 3i - 6i^2 = 5 + 5i(−1+3i)(1−2i)=−1+2i+3i−6i2=5+5i.

(d) i1+i=i(1−i)2=i−i22=1+i2\frac{i}{1 + i} = \frac{i(1 - i)}{2} = \frac{i - i^2}2 = \frac{1 + i}21+ii​=2i(1−i)​=2i−i2​=21+i​.

6 · An equation with the conjugate intermediate

Find all z∈Cz \in \Cz∈C such that z+2zˉ=3−iz + 2\bar z = 3 - iz+2zˉ=3−i.

Solution

Here you cannot "divide by the coefficient", because both zzz and zˉ\bar zzˉ appear. You use the method of coordinates: z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi with x,yx, yx,y real, so zˉ=x−yi\bar z = x - yizˉ=x−yi.

  1. Left-hand side: z+2zˉ=x+yi+2x−2yi=3x−yiz + 2\bar z = x + yi + 2x - 2yi = 3x - yiz+2zˉ=x+yi+2x−2yi=3x−yi.
  2. The equation is 3x−yi=3−i3x - yi = 3 - i3x−yi=3−i. Two complex numbers are equal when they have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts: 3x=33x = 33x=3 and −y=−1-y = -1−y=−1.
  3. So x=1x = 1x=1, y=1y = 1y=1: the only solution is z=1+iz = 1 + iz=1+i.

Check: (1+i)+2(1−i)=1+i+2−2i=3−i(1 + i) + 2(1 - i) = 1 + i + 2 - 2i = 3 - i(1+i)+2(1−i)=1+i+2−2i=3−i.

7 · Two second-degree equations solved with coordinates hard

(a) Find all z∈Cz \in \Cz∈C with z2=2iz^2 = 2iz2=2i. (b) Find all z∈Cz \in \Cz∈C with ∣z∣2+z=7+i|z|^2 + z = 7 + i∣z∣2+z=7+i.

Solution

(a) I write z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi. Then z2=x2−y2+2xyiz^2 = x^2 - y^2 + 2xyiz2=x2−y2+2xyi, and the equation z2=0+2iz^2 = 0 + 2iz2=0+2i becomes the system

{x2−y2=02xy=2\begin{cases} x^2 - y^2 = 0 \\ 2xy = 2 \end{cases}{x2−y2=02xy=2​

From the first, y=xy = xy=x or y=−xy = -xy=−x. With y=−xy = -xy=−x the second gives −2x2=2-2x^2 = 2−2x2=2, that is x2=−1x^2 = -1x2=−1: impossible for real xxx. With y=xy = xy=x the second gives 2x2=22x^2 = 22x2=2, that is x=±1x = \pm 1x=±1. Solutions: z=1+iz = 1 + iz=1+i and z=−1−iz = -1 - iz=−1−i, that is z=±(1+i)z = \pm(1 + i)z=±(1+i). Check: (1+i)2=1+2i+i2=2i(1 + i)^2 = 1 + 2i + i^2 = 2i(1+i)2=1+2i+i2=2i. In lesson L03 you will find these two square roots of 2i2i2i again with polar coordinates; they are needed in Example 4.10 of lesson L04.

(b) ∣z∣2=x2+y2|z|^2 = x^2 + y^2∣z∣2=x2+y2 is real, so ∣z∣2+z=(x2+y2+x)+yi|z|^2 + z = (x^2 + y^2 + x) + yi∣z∣2+z=(x2+y2+x)+yi. Equating real part and imaginary part with those of 7+i7 + i7+i:

{x2+y2+x=7y=1\begin{cases} x^2 + y^2 + x = 7 \\ y = 1 \end{cases}{x2+y2+x=7y=1​

Substituting y=1y = 1y=1: x2+x+1=7x^2 + x + 1 = 7x2+x+1=7, that is x2+x−6=0x^2 + x - 6 = 0x2+x−6=0, that is (x+3)(x−2)=0(x + 3)(x - 2) = 0(x+3)(x−2)=0. Two solutions: z=2+iz = 2 + iz=2+i and z=−3+iz = -3 + iz=−3+i. Check: ∣2+i∣2+2+i=5+2+i=7+i|2 + i|^2 + 2 + i = 5 + 2 + i = 7 + i∣2+i∣2+2+i=5+2+i=7+i and ∣−3+i∣2−3+i=10−3+i=7+i|-3 + i|^2 - 3 + i = 10 - 3 + i = 7 + i∣−3+i∣2−3+i=10−3+i=7+i.

8 · The numbers of modulus 1 hard

(a) Prove that if ∣z∣=1|z| = 1∣z∣=1 then z−1=zˉz^{-1} = \bar zz−1=zˉ. (b) Use it to compute the inverse of 35+45i\frac 35 + \frac 45 i53​+54​i.

Solution

(a) If ∣z∣=1|z| = 1∣z∣=1, then also ∣z∣2=1|z|^2 = 1∣z∣2=1, and the inverse formula gives z−1=zˉ∣z∣2=zˉ1=zˉz^{-1} = \frac{\bar z}{|z|^2} = \frac{\bar z}1 = \bar zz−1=∣z∣2zˉ​=1zˉ​=zˉ. In other words, zzˉ=∣z∣2=1z\bar z = |z|^2 = 1zzˉ=∣z∣2=1.

(b) ∣35+45i∣=925+1625=2525=1\left|\frac 35 + \frac 45 i\right| = \sqrt{\frac 9{25} + \frac{16}{25}} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{25}} = 1​53​+54​i​=259​+2516​​=2525​​=1. So the inverse is the conjugate: 35−45i\frac 35 - \frac 45 i53​−54​i. Check: (35+45i)(35−45i)=925+1625=1\left(\frac 35 + \frac 45 i\right)\left(\frac 35 - \frac 45 i\right) = \frac 9{25} + \frac{16}{25} = 1(53​+54​i)(53​−54​i)=259​+2516​=1. In the plane, the numbers of modulus 1 form the unit circle, the protagonist of lesson L03.

9 · Two more sets intermediate

Draw: (a) D={z∈C∣Im⁡(zˉ+2i)>0}D = \{z \in \C \mid \operatorname{Im}(\bar z + 2i) > 0\}D={z∈C∣Im(zˉ+2i)>0}; (b) E={z∈C∣∣z∣=∣z−2i∣}E = \{z \in \C \mid |z| = |z - 2i|\}E={z∈C∣∣z∣=∣z−2i∣}.

Solution

(a) With z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi: zˉ+2i=x−yi+2i=x+(2−y)i\bar z + 2i = x - yi + 2i = x + (2 - y)izˉ+2i=x−yi+2i=x+(2−y)i, so Im⁡(zˉ+2i)=2−y\operatorname{Im}(\bar z + 2i) = 2 - yIm(zˉ+2i)=2−y. The condition 2−y>02 - y > 02−y>0 is y<2y < 2y<2: the half-plane below the horizontal line Im⁡(z)=2\operatorname{Im}(z) = 2Im(z)=2, line excluded. Watch out for the conjugate: it changes the sign of yyy, and this is why the half-plane lies below and not above.

(b) ∣z∣|z|∣z∣ is the distance from 000, ∣z−2i∣|z - 2i|∣z−2i∣ the distance from 2i2i2i: the points equidistant from 000 and from 2i2i2i lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, that is on the horizontal line Im⁡(z)=1\operatorname{Im}(z) = 1Im(z)=1. With the computations: x2+y2=x2+(y−2)2x^2 + y^2 = x^2 + (y - 2)^2x2+y2=x2+(y−2)2, that is y2=y2−4y+4y^2 = y^2 - 4y + 4y2=y2−4y+4, that is y=1y = 1y=1.

10 · As at the exam: find zzz exam style

Find the number z∈Cz \in \Cz∈C such that (1+i)(2−i) z=(3+i)(1−i)(1 + i)(2 - i)\,z = (3 + i)(1 - i)(1+i)(2−i)z=(3+i)(1−i). Possible answers: (a) 1−i1 - i1−i; (b) 1+i1 + i1+i; (c) 2−i2 - i2−i; (d) −1+i-1 + i−1+i; (e) 10−10i10 - 10i10−10i.

Solution
  1. I simplify the two sides. (1+i)(2−i)=2−i+2i−i2=3+i(1 + i)(2 - i) = 2 - i + 2i - i^2 = 3 + i(1+i)(2−i)=2−i+2i−i2=3+i. (3+i)(1−i)=3−3i+i−i2=4−2i(3 + i)(1 - i) = 3 - 3i + i - i^2 = 4 - 2i(3+i)(1−i)=3−3i+i−i2=4−2i.
  2. I divide. (3+i)z=4−2i(3 + i)z = 4 - 2i(3+i)z=4−2i, so
    z=4−2i3+i=(4−2i)(3−i)9+1=12−4i−6i+2i210=10−10i10=1−i.z = \frac{4 - 2i}{3 + i} = \frac{(4 - 2i)(3 - i)}{9 + 1} = \frac{12 - 4i - 6i + 2i^2}{10} = \frac{10 - 10i}{10} = 1 - i.z=3+i4−2i​=9+1(4−2i)(3−i)​=1012−4i−6i+2i2​=1010−10i​=1−i.
  3. Check. (3+i)(1−i)=3−3i+i−i2=4−2i(3 + i)(1 - i) = 3 - 3i + i - i^2 = 4 - 2i(3+i)(1−i)=3−3i+i−i2=4−2i. Correct: the answer is (a).

As a check, or as an alternative strategy in the quiz, you can multiply the other answers by 3+i3 + i3+i: (b) gives 2+4i2 + 4i2+4i, (c) gives 7−i7 - i7−i, (d) gives −4+2i-4 + 2i−4+2i, (e) gives 40−20i40 - 20i40−20i. None is 4−2i4 - 2i4−2i. Answer (e) is the trap for those who forget to divide by ∣3+i∣2=10|3 + i|^2 = 10∣3+i∣2=10.

11 · As at the exam: first zzz, then an expression exam style

If (2−i)z=5i(2 - i)z = 5i(2−i)z=5i, then zzˉ+zz\bar z + zzzˉ+z is: (a) 4+2i4 + 2i4+2i; (b) 6+2i6 + 2i6+2i; (c) −4−2i-4 - 2i−4−2i; (d) 555; (e) 4−2i4 - 2i4−2i.

Solution
  1. z=5i2−i=5i(2+i)4+1=i(2+i)=2i+i2=−1+2iz = \frac{5i}{2 - i} = \frac{5i(2 + i)}{4 + 1} = i(2 + i) = 2i + i^2 = -1 + 2iz=2−i5i​=4+15i(2+i)​=i(2+i)=2i+i2=−1+2i. Check: (2−i)(−1+2i)=−2+4i+i−2i2=5i(2 - i)(-1 + 2i) = -2 + 4i + i - 2i^2 = 5i(2−i)(−1+2i)=−2+4i+i−2i2=5i.
  2. zzˉ=∣z∣2=(−1)2+22=5z\bar z = |z|^2 = (-1)^2 + 2^2 = 5zzˉ=∣z∣2=(−1)2+22=5.
  3. zzˉ+z=5+(−1+2i)=4+2iz\bar z + z = 5 + (-1 + 2i) = 4 + 2izzˉ+z=5+(−1+2i)=4+2i: answer (a).

Where the others come from: (b) is the result with z=1+2iz = 1 + 2iz=1+2i, that is with a sign mistake; (c) uses z2=−3−4iz^2 = -3 - 4iz2=−3−4i instead of zzˉz\bar zzzˉ; (d) forgets to add zzz; (e) uses zˉ\bar zzˉ instead of zzz in the last sum.

§13

Review questions

self-check

Answer out loud or in writing, then open the answer.

Why does the equation x2=−1x^2 = -1x2=−1 have no real solutions, and how do complex numbers solve it?

The square of a real number is never negative: x2≥0x^2 \ge 0x2≥0 for every x∈Rx \in \Rx∈R. The complex numbers add the symbol iii with i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1: in C\CC the equation has two solutions, iii and −i-i−i.

What is a complex number? What are its real part and its imaginary part?

An object of the form a+bia + bia+bi, with a,ba, ba,b arbitrary reals and iii the imaginary unit (Definition 2.1). The real part is Re⁡(z)=a\operatorname{Re}(z) = aRe(z)=a, the imaginary part is the real number Im⁡(z)=b\operatorname{Im}(z) = bIm(z)=b, without the iii.

How do you multiply two complex numbers?

With the distributive property, each term times each term, then replacing i2i^2i2 with −1-1−1 and collecting: (a+bi)(c+di)=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i(a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i(a+bi)(c+di)=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i. For example (7+i)(4−i)=29−3i(7 + i)(4 - i) = 29 - 3i(7+i)(4−i)=29−3i.

What is ini^nin? How do you compute it for large nnn?

The powers of iii repeat every 4: 1,i,−1,−i1, i, -1, -i1,i,−1,−i. Divide nnn by 4 and look at the remainder rrr: in=iri^n = i^rin=ir. For example i15=i3=−ii^{15} = i^3 = -ii15=i3=−i.

Is C\CC a field? Is it ordered?

It is a field: the nine properties of Proposition 2.2 hold, as in R\RR. It is not ordered: in an ordered field the squares of non-zero numbers are positive, so both 1=121 = 1^21=12 and −1=i2-1 = i^2−1=i2 would be, which is impossible.

What is the conjugate of zzz? When is z=zˉz = \bar zz=zˉ?

zˉ=a−bi\bar z = a - bizˉ=a−bi: you change the sign of the imaginary part. z=zˉz = \bar zz=zˉ if and only if b=0b = 0b=0, that is if and only if zzz is real.

What is the modulus of zzz and what does it mean in the plane?

∣z∣=a2+b2|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}∣z∣=a2+b2​, a non-negative real number, zero only for z=0z = 0z=0. It is the distance of the point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) from the origin, by Pythagoras' theorem.

What is zzˉz\bar zzzˉ? Why is it important?

zzˉ=a2+b2=∣z∣2z\bar z = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2zzˉ=a2+b2=∣z∣2: it is always a non-negative real number. Multiplying by the conjugate removes the iii, and it is the trick on which inverse and division are based.

What is the inverse of z≠0z \neq 0z=0? How do you check it?

z−1=zˉ∣z∣2z^{-1} = \frac{\bar z}{|z|^2}z−1=∣z∣2zˉ​. Check: z⋅zˉ∣z∣2=∣z∣2∣z∣2=1z \cdot \frac{\bar z}{|z|^2} = \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2} = 1z⋅∣z∣2zˉ​=∣z∣2∣z∣2​=1. For example (2+i)−1=2−i5(2 + i)^{-1} = \frac{2 - i}5(2+i)−1=52−i​.

How do you compute wz\frac{w}{z}zw​?

You multiply numerator and denominator by zˉ\bar zzˉ: the denominator becomes the real number ∣z∣2|z|^2∣z∣2 and you divide the real part and the imaginary part of wzˉw\bar zwzˉ by it. At the end you check by multiplying by zzz.

What are the real axis and the imaginary axis of the complex plane?

The real axis (horizontal) is the set of real numbers, b=0b = 0b=0; the imaginary axis (vertical) is the set of numbers bibibi, a=0a = 0a=0. The number a+bia + bia+bi is the point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b).

How do you see the sum of two complex numbers in the plane?

With the parallelogram rule: z1+z2z_1 + z_2z1​+z2​ is the fourth vertex of the parallelogram with vertices 000, z1z_1z1​, z2z_2z2​. For example (1+3i)+(4+i)=5+4i(1 + 3i) + (4 + i) = 5 + 4i(1+3i)+(4+i)=5+4i.

What figure is {z∈C∣∣z−c∣=r}\{z \in \C \mid |z - c| = r\}{z∈C∣∣z−c∣=r}, with r>0r > 0r>0?

The circle with centre ccc and radius rrr, because ∣z−c∣|z - c|∣z−c∣ is the distance between zzz and ccc. With ≤\le≤ you get the disc, with ≥\ge≥ the outside of the disc (circle included).

§14

Glossary

terms
Imaginary unit iii
The new symbol of the complex numbers, with the rule i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1.
Complex number
Object a+bia + bia+bi with a,ba, ba,b arbitrary reals (Definition 2.1). The set of complex numbers is C\CC.
Real part Re⁡(z)\operatorname{Re}(z)Re(z)
The real number aaa of z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi.
Imaginary part Im⁡(z)\operatorname{Im}(z)Im(z)
The real number bbb of z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi (without the iii).
Purely imaginary
Complex number with zero real part, like 23i23i23i or −i-i−i.
Form a+bia + bia+bi
The way of writing a complex number that separates real part and imaginary part; it is also called algebraic or Cartesian form.
Conjugate zˉ\bar zzˉ
a+bi‾=a−bi\overline{a + bi} = a - bia+bi​=a−bi: you change the sign of the imaginary part; in the plane it is the mirror image with respect to the real axis.

Field
Set with sum and product that have the nine properties of Proposition 2.2: Q\QQ, R\RR, C\CC.
Ordered field
Field with a notion of greater and smaller compatible with the computations; R\RR is one, C\CC is not.
Complex plane
The plane in which a+bia + bia+bi is the point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b), or the vector from the origin to (a,b)(a, b)(a,b).
Real axis
The horizontal axis of the complex plane: the real numbers.
Imaginary axis
The vertical axis of the complex plane: the numbers bibibi.
Parallelogram rule
